reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: The commonest congenital anomaly of the shoulder girdle, in which one scapula sits abnormally high and is often small and malrotated
The elevated scapula produces visible asymmetry, a fullness at the base of the neck, and restricted shoulder abduction
An omovertebral bone or fibrous band connecting the scapula to the cervical spine is present in many cases and further limits movement
It is frequently associated with Klippel-Feil syndrome, scoliosis, and rib anomalies, so the cervical spine should always be assessed
The condition is usually unilateral but can be bilateral, and most cases are sporadic
Limitation of shoulder elevation, rather than pain, is the usual functional complaint
Cosmetic concern and functional restriction together guide the decision on surgical correction
reference.pathophysiology: Sprengel deformity results from failure of the normal caudal descent of the scapula during embryonic development. The scapula forms in the cervical region and normally migrates to its thoracic position by around the third month of gestation; arrested or incomplete descent leaves it elevated, hypoplastic, and often medially rotated. An abnormal osseous, cartilaginous, or fibrous connection (the omovertebral bar) may tether the superomedial scapula to the lower cervical vertebrae, tethering it in position and restricting movement. Because the disturbance occurs during the same period as cervical vertebral segmentation and rib formation, associated anomalies such as Klippel-Feil fusion, scoliosis, and rib defects frequently coexist. Most cases are sporadic.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital muscular torticollis with postural asymmetry
Poland syndrome with shoulder girdle involvement
additionalInvestigations: Shoulder and scapular radiographs to assess position, size, and rotation
Cervical spine imaging to detect Klippel-Feil fusion and an omovertebral bone
Computed tomography to define the omovertebral connection before surgery
Assessment for scoliosis and rib anomalies
Renal ultrasound where associated anomalies suggest a wider spectrum
Assessment of shoulder range of motion and function
redFlags: Coexisting cervical vertebral instability from associated Klippel-Feil syndrome
Neurological compromise related to cervical or brachial plexus involvement
Severe functional restriction limiting activities of daily living
Associated undiagnosed renal or cardiac anomalies
reference.prognosis: The deformity itself is not life-limiting; mild cases need only observation, while surgical repositioning in selected children can improve appearance and shoulder function, with outcome influenced by associated spinal and girdle anomalies.
pitfalls: Failing to image the cervical spine and missing associated Klippel-Feil syndrome
Overlooking an omovertebral bone that limits movement and complicates surgery
Attributing the asymmetry to posture or torticollis
Neglecting associated scoliosis and rib anomalies
Underestimating the psychosocial effect of visible shoulder asymmetry
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Observation with physiotherapy for mild deformity, focusing on maintaining and improving shoulder abduction and range of motion
Surgical repositioning of the scapula (such as a Woodward or Green procedure) in selected children to improve appearance and shoulder function
Excision of the omovertebral bone or fibrous band to relieve tethering and restricted movement
Assess and manage associated cervical spine anomalies (Klippel-Feil), scoliosis and rib defects
Screen for associated renal and other anomalies where a wider malformation spectrum is suspected
Multidisciplinary input from paediatric orthopaedics, spinal surgery and physiotherapy
